name: Escitalopram (Lexapro)
summary: SSRI antidepressant for depression and anxiety. Once-daily, generally well tolerated, with a black box warning for suicidal thoughts in younger patients and risks of sexual side effects, QTc prolongation, and withdrawal if stopped too quickly.
description: Escitalopram (Lexapro) is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) used to treat depression and anxiety disorders. It’s taken once daily and works slowly over weeks, not minutes. Most people notice fewer mental spirals, more emotional bandwidth, and less background dread as it kicks in. Common trade-offs include nausea in the first week or two, sleep changes, and sexual side effects. At higher doses or in medically vulnerable patients, escitalopram can prolong the QT interval on EKG. Like all antidepressants, it carries a boxed warning about suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, teens, and young adults—so close monitoring early in treatment and after dose changes is non-negotiable.
patient_summary: Escitalopram (Lexapro) is a once-daily antidepressant that helps with depression and anxiety over time. It doesn’t work like Xanax—there’s no quick calm-down effect—but over 2 to 6 weeks, many people feel less overwhelmed, less stuck in their head, and more like themselves again. Upsides: simple dosing, usually pretty well tolerated, and widely used. Downsides: nausea or jitteriness during the first week or two, sexual side effects (low libido or delayed orgasm), and withdrawal symptoms if it’s stopped too fast. For younger people (especially under 25), energy can improve before mood fully lifts, which is why we watch closely for any increase in suicidal thoughts at the beginning or when changing the dose.

linked_conditions.context: FDA-approved for acute and maintenance treatment of unipolar major depressive disorder in adults and adolescents ≥12. Considered a first-line SSRI in most depression guidelines.
FDA-approved for GAD in adults and children ≥7. First-line SSRI for chronic, excessive worry with somatic tension.
Off-label for OCD. Often requires higher doses and longer trials (≥6–12 weeks at maximum tolerated dose) than for depression.
Off-label for panic disorder with or without agoraphobia. Start low to avoid early activation, then titrate slowly.
Off-label option for social anxiety disorder. Useful for generalized social anxiety with performance and interaction fears.
Off-label SSRI for PTSD when first-line agents (sertraline, paroxetine, fluoxetine, venlafaxine) are not tolerated or ineffective.
Off-label SSRI often requiring higher doses and 12–16 week trials, paired with CBT specialized for BDD.
Alternative off-label antidepressant for bulimia nervosa when fluoxetine is not tolerated, always alongside psychotherapy and nutritional rehabilitation.
Off-label option that may reduce binge frequency as part of a broader treatment plan (therapy, nutrition, coping skills).
Off-label for PMDD using continuous daily dosing, luteal-phase dosing, or symptom-onset dosing.
Off-label use in premature ejaculation by delaying ejaculation through serotonergic mechanisms.
Off-label non-hormonal option for menopausal hot flashes when hormone therapy is not desired or is contraindicated.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to escitalopram, citalopram, or any component of the formulation
Use of monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) intended to treat psychiatric disorders, concurrently or within 14 days of discontinuing either escitalopram or the MAOI
Initiation of escitalopram in a patient receiving IV methylene blue
Known QT-interval prolongation or congenital long QT syndrome (per Canadian labeling)
History of serotonin syndrome with an SSRI or other serotonergic agents (relative contraindication)
Escitalopram is not approved for use in pediatric patients <7 years of age

efficacy_response.metric: Clinical response in major depression at 8–12 weeks
efficacy_response.comparison_data: Typical placebo response ≈35–40% in similar trials (estimated NNT ≈6–8 for response).
efficacy_response.patient_text: In large studies, a little over half of people with depression taking escitalopram improved significantly, compared with about one-third to two-fifths on placebo. Put simply: for every 6–8 people treated, one extra person gets a clear benefit because of the medication.
efficacy_response.citation_tag: Representative escitalopram SSRI MDD trial data; numbers rounded for patient education.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Well absorbed after oral dosing; tablets and oral solution are bioequivalent.
pharmacokinetics.onset: Biologic steady state reached in about 1 week; clinical mood and anxiety benefits typically emerge over 2–6 weeks.
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: About 5 hours after dosing in adults (around 3 hours in adolescents).
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Approximately 27–32 hours in adults; prolonged by ~50% in older adults and doubled in hepatic impairment.
pharmacokinetics.duration_IR: Once-daily dosing provides 24-hour coverage due to long half-life.
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatically metabolized primarily via CYP2C19 and CYP3A4 to S-desmethylcitalopram (S-DCT), then via CYP2D6 to S-didesmethylcitalopram (S-DDCT). Metabolites contribute minimally to antidepressant effect.
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Eliminated in urine mainly as metabolites; ~8% excreted as unchanged drug.
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Food does not meaningfully alter exposure; can be taken with or without food.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Escitalopram is a daily SSRI used to treat depression and anxiety disorders. It does its best work as a long-game medication: taken consistently over weeks to rebalance serotonin circuits, not as a quick rescue for panic in the moment.
items: {link:condition:major-depressive-disorder:Major Depressive Disorder (MDD)}: Persistent low mood, loss of interest, appetite and sleep changes, low energy, guilt, and hopelessness.
{link:condition:generalized-anxiety-disorder:Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD)}: Chronic, hard-to-shut-off worry with muscle tension, restlessness, and poor sleep.
Mixed depression + anxiety: Very common in real life—escitalopram works well when both are present.
Maintenance treatment: Keeping depression and anxiety in remission after a successful acute course.
off_label: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), often requiring higher doses and longer treatment trials.
Panic disorder with or without agoraphobia.
Body dysmorphic disorder (often with CBT specialized for BDD).
Bulimia nervosa and binge-eating disorder (always alongside therapy and nutrition work).
Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (continuous, luteal-phase, or symptom-onset dosing).
Vasomotor symptoms of menopause (hot flashes) when hormone therapy is not an option.

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Escitalopram changes things slowly. You usually don’t wake up one morning magically better; it’s more like realizing, a few weeks in, that your brain hasn’t been screaming at you all day.

quotes: My stomach felt off and I had a mild headache at first.
I felt a little wired and restless before I actually felt calmer.
Sleep was weird—either more tired than usual or a bit revved up at night.
items.note: Startup side effects (nausea, headache, jitteriness, sleep changes) are common early and usually fade within 1–3 weeks.

quotes: The volume on my worry dropped from a 10 to maybe a 5.
The same stress is still there, but it doesn’t knock me flat anymore.
I caught myself actually laughing and realized I hadn’t done that in a while.
My sex drive dipped and that was annoying.
I can get aroused but orgasm takes way longer, or sometimes doesn’t happen.
We talked about it instead of pretending it wasn’t happening, which helped.
items.note: Sexual side effects (low libido, delayed orgasm, difficulty with erection or lubrication) are common with SSRIs. They’re real and they’re worth talking about—dose adjustments and strategy changes are often possible.

quotes: I feel less panicky, but sometimes also a bit emotionally muted.
I don’t cry as easily, in good and bad ways.
I feel more stable, just not as intense.
items.note: Some people experience emotional blunting—less emotional pain, but also less intensity in general. This can sometimes be managed by dose changes, therapy, or switching medications.

quotes: When I missed a few doses I felt dizzy and got weird ‘brain zaps.’
I felt off-balance, nauseated, and extra emotional after I quit suddenly.
Slowing the taper made everything way more tolerable.
items.note: Withdrawal (discontinuation) symptoms are uncomfortable but preventable. They’re a sign the dose changed too quickly, not that your brain is broken.

quotes: My energy came back before my mood fully lifted, which felt like a risky combo.
We had more check-ins in the first month, which actually made me feel safer.
My parents were looped in so I wasn’t trying to manage everything alone.
items.note: In children, teens, and young adults, antidepressants can increase suicidal thoughts in the first few months, especially when energy improves before mood. That’s why close monitoring and honest communication are essential.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Escitalopram is a slow but steady builder, not a fast-acting rescue.
key_points: 1–2 weeks: Some people notice small shifts—slightly lighter mood, improved sleep, fewer intense spikes.
2–4 weeks: Clearer changes in worry, mood, and reactivity for many patients.
6–8 weeks: Full antidepressant and GAD effect for most people at a therapeutic dose.
OCD/PTSD/BDD: Often need 10–12+ weeks at higher doses before calling it a failed trial.
Once-daily dosing: Long half-life allows flexible morning or evening dosing based on side effects.

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Escitalopram performs similarly to other modern SSRIs but tends to be on the better-tolerated side. When combined with therapy, sleep hygiene, exercise, and structure, response rates are clinically meaningful.
sections.clinical_details: Across randomized trials in unipolar depression, roughly 55–60% of patients on escitalopram achieve at least a 50% symptom reduction by 8–12 weeks, versus about 35–40% on placebo. Remission rates are lower but still clinically significant. In GAD and other anxiety disorders, effect sizes are comparable to other first-line SSRIs.

citation.title: Escitalopram in major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders
citation.pmid: Representative data set; see FDA label and guideline summaries

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Suicidal thoughts and behaviors: Antidepressants increased the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in pediatric and young adult patients in short-term studies.
sections.black_box: Closely monitor all antidepressant-treated patients, especially children, adolescents, and young adults, for clinical worsening and for the emergence of suicidal thoughts and behaviors, particularly during the first few months of therapy or at times of dose changes. Escitalopram is not approved for use in pediatric patients <7 years of age.
other: QT prolongation: Escitalopram can prolong QTc in a dose-related fashion, particularly above 20 mg/day or in patients with multiple risk factors (electrolyte disturbances, structural heart disease, other QT-prolonging drugs).
Serotonin syndrome: Risk increases when combined with other serotonergic drugs (MAOIs, linezolid, triptans, tramadol, St. John’s wort, other SSRIs/SNRIs).
Hyponatremia/SIADH: Particularly in older adults, low body weight, diuretic use, or prior history of hyponatremia.
Bleeding risk: SSRIs can increase bleeding risk, especially when combined with NSAIDs, antiplatelets, or anticoagulants.
Mania/hypomania: Antidepressants can precipitate mania or mixed states in patients with bipolar disorder or vulnerable mood architecture.
Bone health: Long-term SSRI use is associated with increased fragility fracture risk, especially in older adults.
patient_counseling: Report any new or worsening suicidal thoughts, agitation, or extreme mood swings immediately—especially in the first 1–2 months or around dose changes.
Tell your clinician about all medications and supplements, especially other antidepressants, migraine medications, pain medications, and blood thinners.
Seek urgent care for signs of serotonin syndrome: fever, sweating, racing heart, rigid muscles, confusion, or severe agitation.
Contact your clinician for confusion, severe headaches, falls, or new balance problems—these can be signs of low sodium or other complications.
If you have or may have bipolar disorder, antidepressants should be handled carefully and usually combined with a mood stabilizer.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most side effects are mild to moderate and front-loaded in the first few weeks. Sexual side effects and emotional blunting can persist and are often under-reported unless we ask directly.
plain_language_list: Nausea or upset stomach (especially at the start)
Headache and feeling a bit foggy at first
Sleep changes: more tired or more wired
Sexual side effects: low libido, delayed orgasm, erectile issues
Weight changes: usually modest, can go up or down

common.patient_note: Often improves after the first 1–2 weeks. Taking with food or at night can help.
Usually fades with time; simple analgesics and good hydration often help.
If it makes you sleepy, take it at night. If it wires you, take it in the morning.
Low libido and delayed orgasm are widely reported. This is a medical side effect, not a character flaw, and it’s absolutely something to bring up.
Some people feel less emotionally volatile but also less intense. Dose tweaks can sometimes find a better balance.

serious: Serotonin syndrome: anxiety, agitation, tremor, clonus, fever, autonomic instability—medical emergency.
QT prolongation and rare torsades de pointes in high-risk patients or at high doses.
Severe hyponatremia/SIADH: confusion, seizures, falls, especially in older adults.
Severe bleeding events (GI bleeding, intracranial hemorrhage) when combined with other bleeding-risk medications.
Mania or hypomania: decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, impulsivity, grandiosity in susceptible individuals.
Severe cutaneous reactions (Stevens–Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis)—very rare but serious.

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Escitalopram is metabolized by CYP2C19 and CYP3A4 and has serotonergic and QT-prolonging potential. The big worries: serotonin syndrome, excessive sedation, and QTc synergy.

items.with: MAOIs (including linezolid and methylene blue at higher/systemic doses)
items.risk: Life-threatening serotonin syndrome with agitation, hyperthermia, and autonomic instability.
items.action: Contraindicated. Allow at least 14 days between escitalopram and MAOI in either direction.

items.with: Other serotonergic agents (SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs, triptans, tramadol, lithium, St. John’s wort)
items.risk: Increased risk of serotonin syndrome; overlapping side effects (GI upset, agitation).
items.action: Use lowest effective doses, avoid duplicate therapy, and monitor closely for serotonin toxicity.

items.with: QT-prolonging medications (certain antipsychotics, macrolide antibiotics, methadone, some antiarrhythmics)
items.risk: Additive QTc prolongation and rare torsades de pointes, especially at higher escitalopram doses or with electrolyte abnormalities.
items.action: Avoid high-dose escitalopram; correct electrolytes; consider baseline and follow-up ECGs.

items.risk: Increased risk of bruising and bleeding, including GI bleeding.
items.action: Use gastroprotection if appropriate; counsel on bleeding signs (black stools, nosebleeds, easy bruising).

items.with: Strong CYP2C19 or CYP3A4 inhibitors (omeprazole, fluconazole, some HIV protease inhibitors, macrolides)
items.risk: Higher escitalopram levels, increased risk of side effects and QTc changes.
items.action: Consider lower escitalopram doses and closer monitoring.

items.with: Alcohol and sedatives (benzodiazepines, opioids, sedating antihistamines)
items.risk: Increased sedation, falls, cognitive impairment; can worsen depression and judgment.
items.action: Encourage minimal or no alcohol and careful use of other sedatives; avoid combining with high-risk opioid regimens whenever possible.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Escitalopram is not chemically addictive, but your brain does adapt to it. Stopping suddenly can feel rough and is often misread as ‘my depression instantly came back’ when it’s actually withdrawal.
key_points: If treatment has lasted ≥4 weeks, taper instead of stopping abruptly.
Typical adult taper: reduce dose by about 25% every 1–2 weeks; slower if sensitive or on high doses.
For long-term treatment (>6–12 months), some patients need multi-month tapers.
Common withdrawal symptoms: dizziness, electric ‘brain zaps,’ nausea, flu-like symptoms, insomnia, irritability, and emotional swings.
If significant withdrawal occurs, go back to the last comfortable dose and taper more gradually.
Consider timing tapers during lower-stress life periods when possible.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Escitalopram is usually taken once daily, morning or evening. For anxiety-prone patients, starting low and going slow is key to avoiding early activation and dropout.

adult.depression_initial: 10 mg PO once daily; consider 5 mg once daily in very anxious or medication-sensitive patients.
adult.depression_titration: Increase by 10 mg/day after at least 1 week if needed and tolerated.
adult.depression_max: 20 mg/day per labeling; some clinicians cautiously use up to 30 mg/day with ECG monitoring in selected patients.
adult.gad_titration: Increase by 5–10 mg/day at intervals of at least 1 week based on response and tolerability.
adult.ocd_titration: Increase by 10 mg/day every 1–2 weeks as tolerated.
adult.ocd_max: Up to 40 mg/day off-label in refractory cases, with careful monitoring for QTc changes and side effects.
adult.panic_initial: 5 mg PO once daily for 3–7 days to reduce activation.
adult.panic_titration: Increase to 10 mg/day, then up to 20 mg/day after at least 1 week if needed.
adult.panic_max: 20 mg/day typical; higher doses rarely used and should be specialist-managed.
adult.ptsd_titration: Increase by 5–10 mg/day every 1–4 weeks based on response and tolerability.
adult.ptsd_max: 20–40 mg/day off-label, with ECG monitoring at higher doses.
adult.social_anxiety_titration: Increase to 20 mg/day after at least 4 weeks if partial response.
adult.pmdd_continuous: 5–10 mg PO once daily, increasing to 20 mg/day over the first month if needed.
adult.pmdd_luteal_phase: 5–10 mg PO once daily, starting about 14 days before menses and stopping at onset of bleeding; may increase to 20 mg/day in the luteal phase.
adult.pmdd_symptom_onset: 5–10 mg PO once daily from onset of symptoms until a few days after menses starts; may increase to 20 mg/day if needed.
adult.premature_ejaculation_max: 20 mg PO once daily after 3–4 weeks if needed and tolerated.
adult.vasomotor_initial: 10 mg PO once daily for menopausal hot flashes.
adult.vasomotor_max: Increase to 20 mg/day after about 4 weeks if symptoms are not adequately controlled and tolerated.

sections.simple_explanation: Start low, give it time, and only push the dose if you’ve given the current dose a fair trial (usually several weeks) and still have significant symptoms.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Escitalopram is often a reasonable SSRI choice in pregnancy and lactation when treatment is clearly needed. The bigger risk in many cases is untreated depression or anxiety, not the medication itself.
sections.pregnancy: SSRIs, including escitalopram, have been studied extensively. Overall, major birth defect risk does not appear dramatically increased once confounders are accounted for. Third-trimester exposure can lead to neonatal adaptation syndrome (jitteriness, poor feeding, respiratory distress) that usually resolves within days to weeks. Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN) is a rare but reported risk. Do not automatically stop escitalopram solely because of pregnancy—this is a shared decision balancing relapse risk against fetal and neonatal risks.
sections.lactation: Escitalopram and its active metabolite are present in breast milk at low relative infant doses (generally under or around 5–10% of the weight-adjusted maternal dose). Most breastfed infants do well, but monitoring is recommended for sedation, feeding difficulty, poor weight gain, or unusual irritability. For a patient already stable on escitalopram during pregnancy, continuing postpartum while breastfeeding is often reasonable.
sections.pediatrics: Approved in the US for MDD in patients ≥12 and for GAD in patients ≥7. Start at lower doses, titrate slowly, and monitor closely for activation, behavioral changes, and suicidal thoughts. Combine with psychotherapy whenever possible.
sections.geriatrics: Older adults have higher escitalopram exposure (higher AUC and longer half-life). Start low (eg, 5 mg/day), go slow, and monitor closely for hyponatremia, falls, and QTc prolongation. SSRIs, including escitalopram, are flagged in Beers/STOPP criteria for fracture and hyponatremia risk.
sections.hepatic: In Child-Pugh A–C, start 5 mg once daily and titrate more slowly with extended intervals (eg, ≥2 weeks between increases). Avoid exceeding the usual indication-specific maximum dose. Monitor for excessive sedation and QTc changes.
sections.renal: Mild to moderate impairment: no routine dose adjustment but monitor for side effects. Severe impairment or dialysis: consider starting at 5 mg/day and titrate cautiously with close monitoring, given data suggesting higher sudden cardiac death risk with citalopram/escitalopram in hemodialysis patients.
sections.other: CYP2C19 poor metabolizers and older adults may have higher levels at a given dose; consider lower maximum doses (eg, 10–20 mg/day) and/or ECG monitoring if other QT risk factors are present.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Suicidality and clinical worsening: especially in children, adolescents, and young adults during the first 1–2 months and around dose changes.
Mood, anxiety, and functioning: use rating scales (PHQ-9, GAD-7, OCD/PTSD scales) alongside subjective reports.
Screen for bipolar disorder before initiating therapy: personal or family history of mania, hypomania, or bipolar disorder.
Electrolytes (especially sodium): at baseline and as clinically indicated in older adults, diuretic users, or those with prior hyponatremia.
ECG: in patients with cardiac disease, multiple QT-prolonging medications, electrolyte disturbances, or when using doses above standard ranges.
Bleeding: bruising, GI bleeding, heavy menstrual bleeding, especially with NSAIDs, antiplatelets, or anticoagulants.
Weight, sleep, and sexual function: routinely ask—patients often won’t volunteer this unless you do.
Withdrawal symptoms: during dose reductions; adjust taper speed if symptoms are significant.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Multiple oral formulations make dosing flexible across ages and clinical scenarios.
items: Tablets (US): 5 mg, 10 mg, 20 mg (Lexapro brand and generics).
Tablets (Canada and other markets): additional strengths such as 15 mg tablets and orally disintegrating tablets depending on manufacturer.
Oral solution: escitalopram oral solution at various strengths (eg, 5 mg/5 mL, 10 mg/10 mL) for patients who cannot swallow tablets or need fine-tuned dosing.
Capsule formulations (in some markets): 15 mg capsules designed for once-daily use.

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Escitalopram is the S-enantiomer of citalopram and selectively blocks the serotonin transporter (SERT), increasing serotonin levels in key mood and anxiety circuits. It has minimal direct activity at other receptors (adrenergic, histaminic, muscarinic, dopaminergic), which is part of why its side effect profile is relatively clean compared with older antidepressants. Over weeks, enhanced serotonin signaling helps down-regulate overactive threat circuitry and stabilize mood.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Escitalopram is a workhorse, first-line SSRI for both depression and generalized anxiety. It tends to be chosen when you want: (1) a relatively simple interaction profile, (2) flexible once-daily dosing, and (3) a good balance between efficacy and tolerability. It’s not a ‘rescue’ medication for acute panic in the moment—that’s where non-pharmacologic grounding skills or, in selected cases, short-term benzodiazepine use may come in. But for long-term stabilization of mood and anxiety, escitalopram fits squarely in the core of modern treatment algorithms.

seo.title: Escitalopram (Lexapro): Uses, Dosing, Side Effects, Suicidality & Withdrawal
seo.description: Psychiatry-focused guide to escitalopram (Lexapro): how it works, evidence-based dosing for depression and anxiety, suicidal thoughts warning in younger patients, sexual side effects, QTc risk, withdrawal, and safe tapering strategies.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.a: Escitalopram is an SSRI used to treat major depression and generalized anxiety disorder. It is also commonly used off-label for panic disorder, social anxiety, OCD, PTSD, and PMDD. It’s taken once daily to provide long-term mood and anxiety stabilization, not quick rescue relief.

faqs.q: How long does escitalopram take to work?
faqs.a: Most people do not feel much in the first week besides side effects. Some notice small shifts by week 2. A more solid response often shows up between weeks 4 and 6, with ongoing improvements through week 8 or beyond. Conditions like OCD and PTSD may need 10–12+ weeks at a full dose before we judge the trial.

In children, teens, and young adults, studies show a small but real increase in suicidal thoughts and behaviors when starting antidepressants compared with placebo. The risk is highest in the first few months and around dose changes. This doesn’t mean you shouldn’t take it—it means we monitor more closely, make sure you’re not carrying this alone, and adjust quickly if things worsen.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects?
faqs.a: The big ones early on are nausea, headache, mild jitteriness or fatigue, and sleep changes. Over time, sexual side effects (low libido, delayed orgasm) and emotional blunting are the most common long-term complaints. Most people do not gain a large amount of weight, but small shifts up or down can happen.

It’s generally more weight-neutral than some other antidepressants, but mild weight gain or loss can occur. Appetite may change in either direction. Big, rapid weight shifts should prompt a check-in with your clinician to see if it’s medication-related, depression-related, or something else entirely.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol while taking escitalopram?
faqs.a: Alcohol plus escitalopram isn’t a fatal combination the way alcohol plus benzodiazepines or opioids can be, but it can absolutely worsen depression, anxiety, sleep, and impulsivity. If you drink, doing so lightly and occasionally is safer. If you have a history of substance use issues, we usually recommend avoiding alcohol altogether.

faqs.q: What about sexual side effects on Lexapro?
faqs.a: SSRIs, including escitalopram, commonly cause sexual side effects—lower desire, delayed orgasm, or trouble with erection or lubrication. This is extremely common and under-reported. Options include waiting to see if it improves, dose adjustment, timing changes, switching medications, or adding targeted treatments. Don’t suffer in silence—this is exactly the kind of thing we want you to tell us about.

faqs.q: How do I taper off escitalopram safely?
faqs.a: If you’ve been on escitalopram for more than a few weeks, we taper rather than stop cold turkey. A typical taper is 25% dose reduction every 1–2 weeks, slower if you’ve been on higher doses or for years. If you get withdrawal symptoms—brain zaps, dizziness, nausea, or feeling emotionally raw—we usually go back to the last comfortable dose and slow the taper down.

faqs.q: Is escitalopram safe in pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: Many pregnant and breastfeeding patients stay on escitalopram when the benefits outweigh the risks. Untreated depression and anxiety carry their own risks for both parent and baby. There can be newborn adjustment symptoms in late-pregnancy exposure, but stopping abruptly can also be dangerous. This is a nuanced, shared decision with your prescriber and obstetric team—not something to handle alone or suddenly.

faqs.q: Can escitalopram be used with other psychiatric meds?
faqs.a: Often yes. Escitalopram is commonly combined with mood stabilizers (for bipolar depression), atypical antipsychotics (for psychotic features or augmentation), stimulants (for ADHD), or benzodiazepines (short-term, carefully) for severe anxiety. The key is watching for serotonin syndrome, QTc issues, and overlapping side effects. Never add or remove psychiatric meds on your own—always coordinate with your prescriber.

faqs.q: What’s the difference between escitalopram and citalopram?
faqs.a: Escitalopram is essentially the active ‘half’ of citalopram. It tends to be somewhat more potent on a milligram-for-milligram basis, and generally has less QTc prolongation at typical doses compared with high-dose citalopram. In practice, both are SSRIs with similar uses; escitalopram is often favored when QTc or drug interactions are a concern.
